Papa John's and TrueLayer have partnered with Lloyds to demonstrate how a checkout agent can incorporate Pay by Bank for a seamless agentic payment experience. Papa John’s AI agent helps the customer with their order, and then pays straight from the bank account the customer has linked to their Papa John’s account. Linking a bank account, rather than a card, is made possible by open banking technology, and this is the first time it has been combined with AI. When linking their account, the customer sets a spending limit with their bank, which cannot be exceeded by any AI agent - an inbuilt guardrail for the consumer. Authorisation happens within the user's bank app, so no credentials or passwords are ever shared with the agent. TrueLayer, Europe’s leading Pay by Bank network, conducted a pilot with Papa John's that saw an AI agent complete a Pay by Bank payment to a named UK retailer for the first time. It also marked the first use of Lloyd’s variable recurring payment APIs for agentic payments. Conducted through the FCA’s Supercharged Sandbox, the work culminated in TrueLayer sharing its findings and learnings with the FCA and industry at the regulator’s showcase on 26 November. AI agents are expected to handle a growing share of online shopping. TrueLayer is demonstrating that non-card payments can help maintain competition in payment acceptance in the age of AI commerce, and are better suited to agentic payments because consumers can set up mandates with their banks without sharing card details. The customer sets up the mandate once, choosing their own spending limits per merchant or over specific time periods. The bank checks every payment against the customer's limits and declines anything above it. The customer can cancel the mandate with their merchant or from their banking app at any time. Francesco Simoneschi, CEO and co-founder, TrueLayer: "Personal agents are changing the way we shop, and agentic commerce will be more disruptive than eCommerce was in 2000. Consumers want a safe, simple way for their agents to buy on their behalf. Merchants want to keep control of the customer experience while cutting cost and risk. And agents will choose the payment rail that is fastest, most secure and lowest cost, not the one people use out of habit. That's Pay by Bank: instant, secure, and governed by a digital mandate, with spending limits the customer sets with their own bank. Today it's pizza. Tomorrow it's everything else. ”. This showcase demonstrates the potential for Open Banking technology to support agentic payments, which informs the work to create the right conditions and standards needed to adopt this technology fully and safely at scale. Exam Prep: What State Bank Supervisors May Ask About AI
excerpt: Exam Prep: What State Bank Supervisors May Ask About AI. By PYMNTS | November 25, 2026. |. Banks and nonbank financial companies preparing for their next state examination may face a deceptively simple question: Where are you using artificial intelligence (AI)? An institution that says it uses no AI could still be asked for its software and vendor inventories, its list of approved tools and records of recent platform changes. A vendor may have added AI in a routine update, or employees may be using generative AI tools outside approved channels. That is one takeaway from a Nov. 19 analysis by law firm Baker Donelson of the emerging consensus among regulators about how and where to focus oversight of banks’ use of AI. The Conference of State Bank Supervisors ( CSBS ) released its AI supervisory framework in September for state-chartered banks and state-licensed nonbanks, including consumer lenders, mortgage companies and money transmitters. States decide whether and how to use it. The framework also includes supplements on vendor risk, model risk and consumer protection for nonbanks. The state guide is similar to the federal framework the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ( OCC ) issued Nov. 4 for its bank examiners. Both are examiner resources that create no new legal obligations. But Baker Donelson noted a common line of inquiry: Where is AI used, what risks does it create, who oversees it and can the institution show its controls are up to the task? The scope of a state exam will depend on the institution’s size, complexity, risk profile and use of AI. Examiners may ask who owns each application, what data it can access and whether it supports a decision, makes one or acts on its own. A tool that drafts internal emails presents different risks from one that helps decide who gets a loan. The distinction matters because examiners can use the consequences of an error or unauthorized action to determine where a deeper review is warranted. Vendor contracts may come under scrutiny, especially where AI handles sensitive information or influences decisions. Examiners may ask whether vendors can retain or share customer data or use it to train models. They may also look at how institutions monitor performance, handle changes to AI features and respond to incidents. Older agreements may leave those questions unanswered. Existing consumer protection obligations will also shape the review. If an AI tool recommends denying credit, examiners may ask whether the lender can give legally sufficient reasons for the denial and test for discriminatory outcomes. They may request chatbot transcripts, notices or other communications to see whether AI-generated material is accurate and complies with applicable law. For AI agents that can initiate transactions or access internal systems, examiners may look at permission limits, when employees must approve actions, what the system logs and whether staff can reverse an action or halt the tool. Baker Donelson advised institutions to make sure reviewers have the information, authority and opportunity to intervene. Baker Donelson recommended updating the AI inventory to capture employee tools and vendor features, and documenting risks and controls according to potential harm. Institutions should revisit vendor due diligence and contracts for data use, notification of incidents or changes, and termination rights. They should also test customer-facing tools, review AI-generated communications and check whether consequential decisions can be explained. The firm advised banks to use the CSBS document request list to identify gaps before examiners arrive. Institutions should be ready to produce policies, governance records, risk assessments, training materials, test results and management reports. Existing cybersecurity, privacy, model risk and consumer compliance programs can provide a starting point. title: AI could displace 24 million knowledge-worker jobs globally in five years: JP Morgan report
excerpt: HYDERABAD: Artificial intelligence could displace around 24 million knowledge-worker jobs worldwide over the next five years as businesses increasingly turn to automation to reduce labour costs, according to a report by JP Morgan Wealth Management. The report presents an illustrative scenario in which AI could replace approximately 1. 3 per cent of the global knowledge workforce every year over five years. The estimate assumes that half of potential enterprise AI spending goes towards replacing jobs that would otherwise have been filled, with AI costing about half as much as human workers. However, the report cautions that much of the adjustment may happen through vacancies being left unfilled rather than direct layoffs. It warns that concentrated job losses in particular occupations or regions could create significant economic and political pressure. The United States could face a substantial impact, with around 16 million workers potentially affected over five years if two-thirds of displaced positions are located there. This would represent nearly three million workers annually, equivalent to about two per cent of payrolls each year. Follow for more details: munsifdaily. com. JP Morgan said the more likely outcome was a transformation of existing jobs rather than their complete elimination, as AI could automate only a portion of the tasks performed by employees. Currently, only six per cent of working hours in the US are AI-assisted, although nearly two-thirds of tasks could theoretically be exposed to the technology. Wider adoption across industries will be necessary to deliver productivity gains. A concrete example of this shift emerged in May 2023, when IBM CEO Arvind Krishna announced plans to pause hiring for certain back-office positions, particularly in human resources, as AI and automation could potentially replace around 7,800 jobs over five years. He indicated that nearly 30 per cent of non-customer-facing roles could be affected, with some vacancies left unfilled rather than employees being directly laid off. The JP Morgan projections assume significance against this backdrop, particularly for countries such as India, where millions of people work in IT services, business process outsourcing, finance and other knowledge-based sectors. title: Bank of Japan Calls for Stronger Cybersecurity Safeguards Amid Digital Money and AI Expansion
excerpt: Bank of Japan Calls for Stronger Cybersecurity Safeguards Amid Digital Money and AI Expansion. Central bank warns that stablecoins, tokenised deposits and artificial intelligence could create fresh financial and cybersecurity challenges, stressing the need for stronger regulations and institutional cooperation. Latest News Science and Technology Technology. By Bold News Digital On Nov 27, 2026. Share. TOKYO, Nov 27: The Bank of Japan has called for stronger safeguards against emerging financial stability and cybersecurity risks as the growing adoption of digital money and artificial intelligence transforms the global financial system. Kazushige Kamiyama, Executive Director of the Bank of Japan, said on Friday that policymakers and financial institutions must strengthen their defences against risks associated with new forms of digital money and increasingly interconnected financial infrastructure. Speaking at an International Monetary Fund seminar on digital money and payments in Tokyo, Kamiyama highlighted the opportunities offered by technological innovation while cautioning that the expansion of digital financial services must be accompanied by adequate security measures and public confidence. He said emerging forms of digital money, including stablecoins and tokenised deposits, were likely to coexist and interact with one another, creating new challenges for regulators responsible for maintaining financial stability. The rapid development of digital payment systems, blockchain-based financial infrastructure and artificial intelligence is changing how money is transferred, stored and managed. However, these developments also introduce vulnerabilities that could affect financial institutions, businesses and consumers if appropriate safeguards are not established. Kamiyama stressed that technological progress must be supported by trust, emphasising that central bank money would continue to serve as a fundamental foundation of confidence in the monetary system. His remarks come as governments, central banks and financial institutions examine how digital assets and emerging payment technologies can be integrated into existing financial structures without weakening regulatory oversight. Digital currencies create new regulatory challenges One of the central issues highlighted by the Bank of Japan is the growing use of different forms of digital money. Stablecoins are digital tokens generally designed to maintain a stable value by being linked to traditional currencies or other assets. They are increasingly being used for digital payments, cryptocurrency transactions and transfers across blockchain networks. Tokenised deposits, meanwhile, represent conventional bank deposits in digital token form. They are designed to allow financial institutions to use programmable platforms for transferring and settling funds while retaining a connection to the traditional banking system. Although these technologies offer different approaches to digital payments, their growing interaction could make financial markets more complex. For regulators, the challenge will be to ensure that different digital payment systems can operate together without creating fragmentation or undermining confidence in the financial system. If multiple platforms develop independently, differences in technical standards, settlement procedures and regulatory requirements could create difficulties for institutions transferring money between networks. Such fragmentation could also increase operational costs and make it harder for financial authorities to monitor risks across the wider financial system. Kamiyama indicated that policymakers would need to ensure that the diversity of digital money does not create unnecessary divisions or threaten financial stability. The issue is particularly important as financial institutions increasingly explore digital platforms for payments, securities trading and settlement activities.
